Trying to Conceive

Fertility medicines: what each type is for

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A fertility prescription can contain medicines with quite different jobs. One may help a follicle grow, another prevent an early ovulation, and another prepare the womb lining or treat an identified illness. Understanding the purpose matters more than finding the strongest tablet or injection. The right combination depends on the diagnosis and treatment plan for both partners; no medicine guarantees a pregnancy or live birth.

Four purposes within one treatment plan

Fertility medicines broadly help induce or stimulate ovulation, control the timing of an assisted-treatment cycle, support the womb lining or luteal phase, or treat an underlying condition affecting reproduction. These purposes can overlap, but the medicines are not interchangeable. A trigger injection, for example, does not do the same job as several days of follicle stimulation.

Some treatments are tablets; others are injections, nasal sprays or vaginal preparations. The route alone does not measure effectiveness or risk. Brand names, available formulations and approved uses differ between countries and change over time. Use the active ingredient and your own prescription to identify a medicine, rather than an old online brand list.

The diagnosis comes before the drug

Assessment may include ovulation and menstrual history, pregnancy exclusion, ultrasound, appropriate hormone tests, semen assessment and checking whether the fallopian tubes are open. Which tests are useful depends on the situation. A medicine that induces ovulation cannot by itself overcome every tubal, sperm or uterine problem.

Anovulation, unexplained infertility and an IVF cycle need different plans. For example, an oral stimulation medicine with intrauterine insemination (IUI) can be an option for unexplained infertility, while clomiphene with timed intercourse alone has not shown the same benefit. Ask what problem the prescription addresses and what result will lead to continuation, cancellation or a different approach.

Clomiphene citrate

Clomiphene, sometimes known by the brand Clomid, is an oral medicine used for selected ovulation disorders. It changes estrogen signalling so the body releases more hormones that stimulate the ovaries. It is not suitable during pregnancy, and the prescriber checks relevant conditions such as liver disease, unexplained bleeding and certain ovarian cysts before treatment.

Hot flushes, headache, mood changes and ovarian enlargement can occur. Multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) are possible, even though OHSS is more associated with injectable stimulation. If blurred vision, flashes or other visual symptoms develop while taking clomiphene, stop taking it and contact the prescriber promptly for an eye assessment; do not drive with visual disturbance. Do not repeat or increase a course yourself.

Letrozole and the reason for an off-label prescription

Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor originally licensed for breast cancer. Current international guidance prefers it as first-line medicine for anovulatory infertility in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), when there are no other infertility factors. Clomiphene remains an alternative in appropriate circumstances; these are diagnosis-specific choices, not a universal ranking.

Fertility use of letrozole is off label in many places, meaning that this use is outside the local product licence; it does not by itself mean there is no supporting evidence. The clinician should explain the evidence and local rules. Existing pregnancy must be excluded before ovulation induction. Headache, dizziness, fatigue or hot flushes can occur, and treatment still requires an agreed monitoring plan.

FSH, LH and menotrophin injections

Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) encourages follicle development. Examples include recombinant follitropin alfa, such as GONAL-f, and follitropin beta, such as Puregon. Lutropin alfa, such as Luveris, provides luteinising hormone (LH) for selected patients, including severe LH and FSH deficiency; it is not an automatic addition for everyone. Menotrophin, or hMG, such as Menopur, is urine-derived and provides FSH and LH activity.

Urinary origin does not make a preparation universally weaker, and recombinant production does not make it universally better. Selection considers diagnosis, response, availability, cost and the particular formulation. Gonadotropins can be used for selected ovulation induction as well as IVF. They have not disappeared from IUI care, but routine gonadotropin-IUI for unexplained infertility is generally not favoured because of multiple-pregnancy risk and treatment burden.

The hCG trigger has a separate job

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) can provide an LH-like signal for final follicle maturation and timing of ovulation or egg collection after stimulation. Choriogonadotropin alfa, such as Ovitrelle, is a recombinant example; urinary hCG products also exist. The clinic decides whether a trigger is appropriate from the treatment protocol and response, rather than simply adding it because follicles have been stimulated.

An hCG trigger can contribute to OHSS, and the team may withhold it or choose another strategy when risk is high. Some antagonist IVF protocols use a GnRH-agonist trigger instead; that is a different use of the same drug class. Ovitrelle can interfere with pregnancy tests for up to ten days, so test on the clinic's advised date rather than interpreting an early positive as confirmed pregnancy.

GnRH antagonists and agonists control timing differently

GnRH antagonists, such as cetrorelix (Cetrotide) and ganirelix (Orgalutran), block GnRH receptors and help prevent a premature LH surge and ovulation during assisted treatment. They do not replace the FSH medicine that grows follicles. Timing matters; a missed injection needs prompt instructions from the clinic, not an improvised double dose.

GnRH agonists, including buserelin and some leuprorelin or nafarelin preparations, first stimulate and then, with continued use, suppress pituitary signalling. A clinic may use that suppression in a chosen IVF protocol; selected agonists can also be used as a trigger under a different protocol. Nasal sprays and injections are product-specific. Hot flushes, headache and mood symptoms can occur. These medicines also have uses outside fertility treatment, which does not make every product suitable for every IVF plan.

Scheduling and monitoring are part of treatment

A contraceptive pill or progestogen may be prescribed before an assisted-treatment cycle to help schedule it. Temporary suppression can have a practical purpose even when the goal is pregnancy. It is not proof that every person needs the same preparation, nor that taking contraceptives for two months will reliably rescue an unsuccessful clomiphene course.

Ultrasound and, where indicated, blood tests help the team judge follicle growth and safety. Too many developing follicles may mean withholding a trigger or cancelling a cycle. Follow the clinic's advice about avoiding pregnancy or using barrier contraception after cancellation: unprotected intercourse can still result in a high-risk multiple pregnancy. Monitoring reduces risk but cannot eliminate OHSS or guarantee an outcome.

Estrogen prepares the lining in selected protocols

Estradiol may be used to prepare the endometrium in a programmed frozen-embryo-transfer cycle. Tablets, patches or other formulations are chosen according to the protocol. Estrogen treatment is a specific part of that plan, not a general fertility tonic or an automatic treatment for every thin lining, dry vagina or perceived cervical-mucus problem.

The team considers your medical history and the preparation's contraindications and side effects. Tell them about unusual bleeding and any previous clotting problems. Do not add estrogen from another person's prescription or change its stopping date yourself. Symptoms such as dryness may need their own assessment rather than simply more hormones.

Progesterone support is not the same as treating every miscarriage risk

Progesterone is commonly used for luteal support after IVF and in certain embryo-transfer protocols; vaginal preparations and injections are among the options. This differs from giving progesterone for a presumed luteal-phase deficiency in an unstimulated cycle. A single blood result does not reliably establish that diagnosis, and routine treatment of it has not been shown to improve natural-cycle fertility.

Progesterone also has a defined role in some early-pregnancy bleeding pathways. For example, NICE recommends a particular vaginal preparation when a scan confirms an intrauterine pregnancy and there is current bleeding plus a previous miscarriage. This is not a recommendation for everyone trying to conceive or everyone with a past loss. Follow the clinician's assessment, formulation and duration; bleeding or pain still needs assessment rather than being covered up by hormone treatment.

Aspirin and heparin need a specific indication

Aspirin and heparin are sometimes used in pregnancy-related care, but they are not routine fertility boosters. In confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), a specialist may recommend low-dose aspirin with heparin because the diagnosis and pregnancy history justify that approach. APS is not the same as any abnormal clotting test or an inherited thrombophilia.

Routine anticoagulation is not supported for unexplained recurrent miscarriage or simply for inherited thrombophilia without another indication. These medicines can cause bleeding and have other risks. Do not start an over-the-counter aspirin regimen or use leftover injections to improve implantation; ask what diagnosis, expected benefit and safety plan support the prescription.

Antibiotics treat infection, not every infertility problem

Antibiotics may be needed for an identified reproductive-tract infection. Prompt treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease helps prevent further harm, and partner assessment or treatment may be needed for a sexually transmitted infection. Take the prescribed course and follow advice about sex and follow-up.

Antibiotics cannot reverse established tubal scarring, and clearing an infection does not guarantee conception or correct every abnormal semen result. Persistent pain, fever or discharge needs reassessment. Taking antibiotics without an appropriate diagnosis adds side effects and resistance risk without a demonstrated fertility benefit.

Metformin treats selected metabolic and ovulation problems

Metformin can be useful for metabolic indications in PMOS and can have a role in selected ovulation-treatment plans, alone or in combination. More effective ovulation agents may be available for the particular fertility problem. The choice considers metabolic health, other factors and the treatment setting; it is not automatically required for every person with PMOS.

Gastrointestinal effects are common, and longer-term use may warrant attention to vitamin B12 according to risk. Metformin should not be advertised as a general miscarriage-prevention medicine: international guidance has not shown it to prevent late miscarriage in pregnant people with PMOS. Particular IVF adjunct uses are a separate, protocol-specific question. Discuss continuation in pregnancy with the prescriber rather than assuming a universal stop or continue rule.

High prolactin needs a cause-based plan

Excess prolactin can disrupt reproductive hormones in women and men. The clinician checks possible causes, including medicines, thyroid disease and a prolactinoma, rather than treating every isolated result as a tumour. Cabergoline or bromocriptine, both dopamine agonists, can lower prolactin and restore reproductive function when appropriately indicated; cabergoline is often preferred for prolactinoma because of effectiveness and tolerability.

Nausea, vomiting and dizziness can occur, and the treatment and follow-up depend on the cause and tumour characteristics if present. Make a pregnancy plan with the endocrine team: many patients stop dopamine-agonist treatment after pregnancy is confirmed, but some need continued or restarted treatment. New headache or visual changes require prompt advice. Do not stop another medicine that may raise prolactin without its prescriber's involvement.

Thyroid treatment addresses a diagnosed disorder

Both underactive and overactive thyroid disease can affect reproductive health. Levothyroxine replaces missing thyroid hormone in hypothyroidism; hyperthyroidism needs a different, individually selected treatment. A mildly abnormal laboratory value is not by itself a reason for every person trying to conceive to take thyroid medicine.

Before pregnancy and promptly after a positive test, review the treatment and monitoring plan with the clinician. Requirements can change, and untreated disease also carries risks. Do not stop routine prescribed thyroid treatment on your own. A specific exception concerns antithyroid medicines: if fever, a persistent sore throat, yellow skin or eyes, or a dull abdominal ache develops, stop the antithyroid medicine and contact the doctor immediately because rare serious adverse effects are possible. If you cannot get a response that same day, go to an emergency department.

Medicines can help some male hormone disorders

In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, specialist treatment may use hCG and sometimes FSH to support sperm production. Selected men with low testosterone and infertility may be considered for hCG, a selective estrogen-receptor modulator or an aromatase inhibitor after evaluation. These are indication-specific choices, and some uses are off label; they are not a general treatment for all low sperm counts.

External testosterone, including injections or gels used for low-testosterone symptoms, can suppress sperm production and should not be prescribed as fertility treatment when current or future fertility is desired. Tell the clinician about hormones, anabolic steroids and supplements. Evidence for empiric clomiphene in otherwise unexplained male infertility is limited, so both partners' circumstances and other treatment options matter.

Use a written medicine and follow-up plan

Ask the clinic to list the active ingredient, purpose, route, timing, storage, monitoring and what to do after a missed dose. Check injection training and disposal instructions if relevant. Keep the clinic's daytime and out-of-hours contact details, and bring all prescribed, non-prescription and herbal products to the review. An old brand name or a familiar-looking pen is not enough to identify an interchangeable medicine.

For each proposed add-on, ask whether the aim is ovulation, pregnancy, live birth or symptom control, and what evidence applies to your diagnosis. Agree when to review an unsuccessful cycle and how costs and emotional burden affect the plan. Never share, restart, increase or combine fertility medicines without instructions, and do not stop prescribed estrogen or progesterone support because of an early home test.

When symptoms need urgent or emergency care

During or after fertility treatment, promptly contact the clinic or an urgent medical service for abdominal pain or bloating, nausea or vomiting, feeling faint, coughing blood, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or discomfort when passing urine or stool. Possible pregnancy with pelvic pain also needs urgent assessment. Seek emergency care immediately for severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, or pelvic pain with dizziness, light-headedness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion. These are alternatives; you do not need all of them.

After assisted treatment, breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, being very thirsty while passing less urine, swelling anywhere in the body, one-sided lower abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain also require immediate emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; call the local emergency service or arrange safe transport according to its advice. A new symptom should not be dismissed as an expected medication effect, and a negative or early pregnancy test does not rule out a serious complication. For clomiphene visual symptoms, stop the medicine and arrange prompt eye assessment as described above.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current primary guidance separates ovulation induction, cycle control, hormone support and treatment of identified disease.

Examples describe medicine roles, not a personal prescription or dose schedule; licensing and availability vary locally.

Long guideline and product-label sections were checked for the relevant claims; the article does not imply that every medicine suits every diagnosis.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains the whole medicine map so you can discuss purpose, evidence, monitoring and alternatives with your care team. A treatment decision should account for both partners and the goal of a healthy live birth.

When to seek help

Use fertility medicines only under an agreed clinical plan. Stop clomiphene and seek prompt eye assessment for visual symptoms. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, or pelvic pain with dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or confusion requires emergency care. After assisted treatment, chest or upper-back pain, breathing difficulty, intense thirst with reduced urine, swelling anywhere, one-sided lower abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain also requires emergency care. These are independent alternatives; do not wait for all signs or drive yourself.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Identify the purpose and active ingredient of each medicine, not its supposed strength.
  • Ovulation induction, IVF timing, hormone support and underlying-disease treatment are different jobs.
  • Monitoring and a cancellation plan are essential; tablets and injections can both cause harm.
  • Progesterone, aspirin, heparin and metabolic treatments require specific indications rather than universal promises.
  • Know the urgent and emergency warning signs and keep your clinic's contact details available.

Frequently asked questions

What are the main types of fertility medicine?

They include oral or injected ovulation medicines, medicines that control cycle timing, estrogen or progesterone support in selected protocols, and treatment of diagnosed conditions such as infection, high prolactin, thyroid disease or metabolic problems. The combination depends on the cause, not on a standard shopping list.

Is clomiphene the first choice for everyone?

No. It is useful for selected ovulation disorders, but current international guidance prefers letrozole for anovulatory infertility in PMOS, formerly PCOS, without other infertility factors. Unexplained infertility, male hormone disorders and IVF each need their own assessment.

What clomiphene side effects should I report?

Report troublesome symptoms to the prescriber. Visual changes require stopping clomiphene and prompt eye assessment, with no driving while vision is affected. Abdominal swelling or pain can indicate ovarian complications; severe pain or other emergency signs need immediate care. Do not change the next course yourself.

Why is a cancer medicine used to induce ovulation?

Letrozole's effect on estrogen production can be used in a carefully timed ovulation plan. Fertility prescribing is off label in many countries but is supported for specific indications. It must not be taken for ovulation induction when an existing pregnancy is possible without the clinician first excluding pregnancy.

Are gonadotropin injections always better than tablets?

No. FSH, LH and hMG have different roles and require close supervision. They can help selected patients but bring multiple-pregnancy and OHSS risks. Urinary and recombinant preparations are not ranked universally by strength; the diagnosis, protocol and individual response guide selection.

Do progesterone, aspirin or heparin prevent every miscarriage?

No. Progesterone has established treatment-specific uses, including IVF support and a defined early-bleeding pathway in people with a prior miscarriage. Aspirin with heparin may be appropriate for confirmed APS. None should be started as a universal implantation or miscarriage remedy.

Which symptoms need emergency help?

Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain on movement or touch, or pelvic pain with dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or confusion needs emergency assessment. After assisted treatment, chest or upper-back pain, breathing difficulty, intense thirst with less urine, swelling anywhere, one-sided lower abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain also needs emergency help. You do not need all signs; do not drive yourself.

Can fertility medicines also be prescribed for men?

Yes, for selected hormonal causes: hCG, sometimes FSH, or other specialist treatments may help. Treatment of high prolactin or thyroid disease may also matter. External testosterone can suppress sperm production and is not a fertility treatment; a semen or hormone result needs interpretation in the whole couple's assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
